back: Only the thing it is built for. A sandbox egress list stops a send; least privilege stops a write outside its folder. Each layer names what it stops.
Every layer fails sometimes. With several layers, one failure does not decide the outcome.
front: Why stack defenses instead of relying on one strong one?

back: A server that changes what its tools say or do, so the model is steered by the change. A new version is the usual route.
A pin stops a version nobody reviewed from running. It does not read the data the server returns, so an instruction in the data still gets through.
front: What does a pin stop, and what does it not?

back: An agent that can do more than its task needs. A tidy-up task that can empty an archive has excessive agency.
Allow the listing, read in the notes, and write only in the done folder. Refuse everything else by default, including the shell.
front: Which policy is least privilege for a task that moves one note?

back: Attacking it on purpose with a fixed set of attacks, to find what it lets through before someone else does.
front: What is red-teaming your own agent?

back: The share of seeded attack runs in which the attack succeeded. It is a measure of the lab's runs, reported with the number of runs.
front: What does an attack success rate tell you?
